children: Malaysia's central bank will keep its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 2.75% for a seventh consecutive meeting on Thursday and hold it there through 2027, as inflation remains contained and economic growth stays strong, a Reuters poll showed.

Consumer price inflation rose to 1.8% in July, within the central bank's 1.5%-2.5% forecast range, while the economy grew at a stronger-than-expected 6.0% last quarter according to official data. Central bank Governor Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour said recent indicators pointed to growth of around 5% or higher this year.

Fuel subsidies since the start of the six month long Iran war have also supported the economy. Malaysia's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim recently announced the restoration of higher quotas for subsidised petrol and diesel purchases. Malaysia may spend up to 40 billion ringgit ($9.8 billion) on the subsidies, according to an estimate released in July.
All but two of the 31 economists in the August 26-31 Reuters poll forecast Bank Negara Malaysia to keep its overnight policy rate (MYINTR=ECI) unchanged at 2.75% on September 3.

"While economic growth has been stronger than initially expected, strong growth alone does not necessarily warrant an immediate rate increase. The key question is whether the risks that justified last year's precautionary insurance cut have receded sufficiently to warrant its withdrawal," said Woon Khai Jhek, senior economist at RAM Ratings.
"So far, inflation remains relatively contained, reducing the urgency for BNM to begin hiking rates."
The central bank last cut interest rates in July 2025.

Among the 19 economists who provided forecasts through the end of 2027, a strong majority, 12, expected the policy rate to remain unchanged at 2.75%. The remaining seven forecast a 25-basis-point hike to 3.0%.
"Primarily the protection through subsidies, but also the ringgit strength helps keep import inflation pretty low," said Qi Hang Tay, senior analyst at Economist Intelligence Unit.
Although Tay expects oil prices to rise, he notes that the Strait of Hormuz being closed "has not had a large pass-through to energy freight costs or imported input costs."
The Malaysian ringgit is up nearly 1.0% against the dollar for the year.
